label: Polynomials
overview: Polynomial questions on the SAT cover adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing polynomials; factoring; identifying zeros and their multiplicity; and applying the Remainder Theorem. A polynomial p(x) has (x − r) as a factor if and only if p(r) = 0 (the Factor Theorem).

conceptDiagram.caption: The Remainder Theorem: p(r) tells you the remainder when p(x) is divided by (x − r)

keyFormulas.name: Factor Theorem
keyFormulas.latex: p(r)=0 \iff (x-r) \text{ is a factor of } p(x)

workedExamples.problem: If p(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6, verify that x = 3 is a zero and factor completely.

steps.title: Divide out (x − 3) using synthetic or polynomial division

commonMistakes.mistake: Multiplying (a + b)² as a² + b² (forgetting the middle term)
commonMistakes.fix: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Always square both terms AND include twice their product.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing a zero of the polynomial with a factor — saying 'the zero is (x − 3)'
commonMistakes.fix: The zero is the number x = 3. The factor is the expression (x − 3).

quickTip: On SAT polynomial questions, try the Remainder Theorem before long division — it's much faster. If p(r) = 0, you immediately know (x − r) is a factor.
